newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-S&P says Australia state ratings unaffected.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-S&P says Australia state ratings unaffected.

text.p: Standard and Poor's Corp said on Wednesday that a High Court decision on the taxation powers of Australia's states would have no immediate impact on the ratings of any Australian states and territories.
S&P said the High Court decision in effect rendered franchise fees levied by state governments on tobacco, alcohol, and petrol constitutionally invalid.
These fees contributed A$5 billion of revenue to the states and territories in 1996 out of total state taxation of A$30.4 billion and total state government revenues of A$74.8 billion.
However, S&P said its view was based on the Australian government implementing a package of tax measures to offset the impact on state finances of losing the revenue sources.

The Commonwealth plan to increase existing excise taxes on tobacco, alcohol, and petrol and distribute the proceeds to the states would be done in such a way that left them substantially in the same position as before, S&P said.

"In the medium term, the change in the taxation arrangement for tobacco, alcohol, and petrol could have a small to negative influence on the ratings of the Australian states, but at this point this would not be sufficient to lead to a change in the rating of any particular state," the ratings agency said.

The ratings agency lso said the new system would exacerbate the high degree of fiscal imbalance between the Commonwealth and states, increasing the percentage of state revenue received from the Commonwealth.

Being dependent on another government for a large proportion of revenue was negative from a credit perspective, although having a large proportion of revenue independent of local economic conditions was positive, S&P said.
S&P said the negative factors would probably outweigh the positive.

"While this would not be sufficient in itself to cause a change in the existing rating on any state in the foreseeable future, the outcome of these trends in the longer term remain uncertain," S&P said.
